title: SkillScaffold: Scaffolding Agentic Reinforcement Learning with Policy-Adaptive Skill Credit Assignment and Selective Injection

paper.title: SkillScaffold: Scaffolding Agentic Reinforcement Learning with Policy-Adaptive Skill Credit Assignment and Selective Injection
paper.abstract:
Abstract Agentic reinforcement learning (RL) enables large language models (LLMs) to learn from multi-turn interactions with verifiable outcomes. Textual skills can improve exploration by distilling prior interactions into reusable guidance. However, existing skill-based RL approaches often either assume skill injection is beneficial or rely on indirect feedback or rollout-intensive evaluation to assess its utility. Our pilot studies show that rollout-based utility estimation for skill credit assignment is costly and unstable under limited sampling, while skill benefits vary across candidates and depend on the current policy’s competence on each query. To address these challenges, we introduce SkillScaffold , a policy-adaptive training scaffold that combines low-cost skill-utility estimation with selective skill injection. By reusing outcome-verified training trajectories, SkillScaffold generates candidate skills and estimates their utility through outcome-aware likelihood comparisons, without candidate-specific environment rollouts. The resulting utility guides whether and which skill to inject, retaining skill-free execution when no candidate is estimated to help. Joint training enables the Generator to produce skills tailored to the evolving Executor. Scaffolded RL encourages skill internalization for skill-free inference. Experiments on ALFWorld, WebShop, ScienceWorld, and τ 2 \tau^{2} -Bench demonstrate gains over strong agentic-RL and skill-based RL baselines across both short- and long-horizon tasks. Ablations and further analyses support the importance of utility-based selection and abstention.
Our code is available at https://github.com/Vaidurya00/SkillScaffold .

Our code is available at https://github.com/Vaidurya00/SkillScaffold . 1 Introduction Agentic reinforcement learning (RL) enables language-model agents to improve through multi-turn interaction with verifiable environments, but long horizons and sparse outcome rewards make successful behavior difficult to discover and reinforce ( Shao et al., 2024 ; Dong et al., 2026b ) . Textual skills can ease this challenge by compressing trajectories or feedback into reusable procedural guidance for subsequent decisions ( Shinn et al., 2023 ; Zhao et al., 2024 ) . Existing approaches extract, refine, and retrieve such guidance using external memory or teacher models ( Nottingham et al., 2024 ; Fu et al., 2024 ; Chen et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2024 ; Zhou et al., 2025 ; Fang et al., 2026 ) . SkillRL, for example, uses a stronger teacher to build an evolving SkillBank, turning sparse trajectory-level feedback into guidance for subsequent exploration ( Xia et al., 2026 ) . Figure 1: Overview and empirical summary of SkillScaffold . Low-cost, policy-relative skill-utility estimates guide selective skill injection during training, while inference remains skill-free. Across four agentic benchmarks, SkillScaffold consistently outperforms GRPO and SkillRL while injecting skills for only a small fraction of training queries. Recent work shows that a shared policy can generate skills from experience and use them for subsequent problem solving, allowing generation and execution capabilities to co-evolve ( Wang et al., 2026b ; Xia et al., 2026 ; Shi et al., 2026 ; Fan et al., 2026 ; Zhou et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2026 ; He et al., 2026 ) . Complementary work internalizes skill-conditioned behavior via curriculum learning or self-distillation, enabling skill-free inference ( Lu et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026a ) . Building on these directions, we study skills as policy-adaptive training scaffolds , focusing on evaluating and selectively using guidance for the current policy and query. Under this training-time scaffold view, skill credit assignment uses a scalar skill utility for each candidate to determine whether any skill should be used and which one to select. Existing approaches either use generated skills without testing their benefit ( Xia et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026 ) , rely on indirect and delayed feedback ( Shi et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026 ) , or estimate utility through additional skill-conditioned environment rollouts ( Fan et al., 2026 ; He et al., 2026 ; Shen et al., 2026 ) . Our pilot studies show that rollout-based estimates are costly and unstable under limited sampling, while skill benefits vary across candidates and with how reliably the current policy solves each query without skills ( Dong et al., 2026a ) . These findings motivate a low-cost, policy-relative utility signal for candidate ranking and abstention. To address these challenges, we propose SkillScaffold , a policy-adaptive training scaffold for agentic RL, summarized in Figure 1 . Its core idea is to replace candidate-specific environment evaluation with outcome-aware likelihood comparisons on existing training trajectories. A shared policy serves as both an Executor , which collects skill-free Scout trajectories, and a Generator , which produces candidate skills from outcome-labeled Scout evidence. For each candidate, SkillScaffold rescores fixed Scout evidence under candidate-skill and no-skill contexts to obtain a policy-relative utility estimate. This proxy favors increased likelihood of successful behavior and reduced likelihood of observed failures, according to the available outcome evidence. The highest-utility candidate guides fresh Executor rollouts only when its estimated utility is positive; otherwise, execution remains skill-free. Environment rewards supervise the Executor, while skill utility supervises the Generator through role-specific GRPO objectives, enabling the Generator to adapt its guidance to the evolving Executor. Skill-free Scouts and selectively scaffolded Executor trajectories jointly update the shared policy, encouraging skill internalization. At deployment, the Generator and the entire skill pathway are removed. We evaluate SkillScaffold on ALFWorld, WebShop, ScienceWorld, and τ 2 \tau^{2} -Bench, covering diverse multi-turn environments. Across these settings, SkillScaffold improves over strong agentic-RL and skill-based RL baselines under fully skill-free inference. Ablations and further analyses support the importance of utility-based selection and abstention. In summary, the key contributions of this work are as follows: • We identify two key challenges in skill credit assignment: rollout-based evaluation is costly and unstable, while skill benefits depend on both the candidate and how reliably the current policy can solve the query without skills, motivating candidate ranking and abstention. • We propose SkillScaffold , a shared-policy training scaffold that estimates candidate utility through outcome-aware likelihood comparisons on existing trajectories. The resulting signal guides skill selection, abstention, and Generator learning without candidate-specific environment rollouts. • Experiments on ALFWorld, WebShop, ScienceWorld, and τ 2 \tau^{2} -Bench demonstrate improvements over strong agentic-RL and skill-based RL baselines under skill-free inference. Ablations and further analyses support the importance of utility-based selection and abstention. 2 Preliminaries Agentic reinforcement learning with skills. Rollout-based utility estimation is costly and unstable under practical sampling budgets, while skill utility varies across candidates and with the current policy.
